groups.label: Reading
groups.text:
Keeping a Nature Notebook

A nature notebook can help you notice changes in a familiar place. You do not need to travel far or know the names of every plant. (1) _____ A tree outside a window or a patch of grass near a bus stop can give you plenty to observe throughout the year. Even a small area can look different in each season, especially when you return to it regularly.

Choose a regular time to visit. (2) _____ On each visit, write the date and describe the weather before recording what you see. This routine makes it easier to compare one entry with another, even when several weeks have passed between visits. Keep your notebook where you can find it quickly, and take a pencil that works outdoors.

Look closely, but avoid disturbing living things. Notice the shape of leaves, the colour of flowers or the tracks left in soft ground. (3) _____ Instead, make a quick sketch and add a few words about its size and position. A drawing need not be perfect to be useful later. You can add a name when you have checked a reliable guide.

Ask questions as well as recording facts. For example, you might wonder why a shady corner stays damp longer than the path beside it. (4) _____ Return after different kinds of weather and see whether your observations support that first idea. You may discover that you need to change your explanation.

Finally, look back through your pages from time to time. (5) _____ These patterns may be hard to notice during a single visit. Sharing them with a friend can also lead to new questions and give you another reason to keep observing.

options: If you cannot identify something, do not worry.
Always pick flowers to take home for your notebook.
Start with a place you can reach easily.
You may see patterns in the dates and descriptions.
A long journey is necessary for useful observations.
A visit every week or two is enough to begin.
Write down a possible answer, even if you are unsure.
items.why: 后句列举窗外的树等容易到达的观察地点。

groups.label: Reading
groups.text:
Organising a Book Exchange

A book exchange lets readers share stories without buying new copies. A school or neighbourhood group can organise one with a little planning. It helps to choose a place where people can look through books comfortably and speak to one another. (1) _____ Check that everyone can reach it and that there is enough room for tables.

Next, decide what kinds of books to accept. Books should be clean and complete, but they need not be new. (2) _____ Put that information in a short notice so that visitors know what to bring. You might also mention whether books for younger children are welcome.

On the day, arrange the books before visitors arrive. (3) _____ For example, put stories on one table and practical guides on another. Labels will help visitors find the section they want without having to ask for directions. Leave enough space between the tables for people to move around.

Think about what happens when someone brings several books but finds only one to take home. (4) _____ This lets people contribute without feeling they must take the same number away. Explain the arrangement before the exchange begins so that everyone understands it.

Finally, make a plan for any books left at the end. A local library or community group may be able to use some of them, but ask first rather than leaving them at the door. (5) _____ A brief conversation with helpers afterwards can reveal what to change next time and make the next exchange easier to organise.

options: A clear way to do this is to group them by subject.
A hall or a library room may be suitable.
Ask helpers what worked well and what caused difficulty.
You could let visitors donate extra copies without taking others.
The notice can also list any books you cannot take.
All visitors must purchase a new book first.
Hide the books until everyone has left.
items.why: 后句要求核对地点的交通和空间，承接场地建议。
